NewsCultureNews AnalysisPodDonateMarketplace Home › News › American News › Passengers on hantavirus cruise disembark in Canary Islands as US evacuates Americans News Passengers on hantavirus cruise disembark in Canary Islands as US evacuates Americans Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia said most of the ship’s nearly 150 passengers and crew were expected to be evacuated before a final repatriation flight to Australia on Monday. By Roberto Wakerell-Cruz·May 10, 2026·2 min read Passengers from the cruise ship MV Hondius began returning home Sunday after Spanish authorities launched a large-scale evacuation from the Canary Islands following a hantavirus outbreak linked to three deaths. by Taboolaby Taboola Sponsored LinksSponsored Links Promoted LinksPromoted Links You May Like BREAKING: Dem Kissimmee mayor arrested on grand theft, fraud charges: AG UthmeierKissimmee Mayor Jackie Espinosa was arrested on Wednesday morning. Undo The ship arrived near Tenerife after multiple passengers became infected with the rare virus, prompting an international health response. Three people have died so far, including a Dutch husband and wife and a German woman. Spanish officials began removing passengers from the Dutch-flagged vessel Sunday morning. Travelers wearing blue protective suits were transferred by smaller boats to the port of Granadilla before being taken by Spanish military buses to Tenerife South airport for repatriation flights. The first flight carried 14 Spanish passengers to Madrid, where they will quarantine at a military hospital. “Everything is going well,” French evacuee Roland Seitre told AFP before departure, adding that “everyone was great” during the disembarkation. A separate flight transported 27 passengers to the Netherlands, including citizens from Belgium, Greece, Germany, Guatemala, and Argentina, according to Spanish civil protection chief Virginia Barcones. Additional flights for Turkish, British, Irish, and American passengers were also scheduled. Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia said most of the ship’s nearly 150 passengers and crew were expected to be evacuated before a final repatriation flight to Australia on Monday. Health authorities have identified at least 10 affected Canadians. Four remained onboard before the vessel reached the Canary Islands, while six others were either no longer aboard or had close contact with infected individuals. Canadian passengers departing Sunday were seen wearing protective equipment while boarding a flight bound for Saguenay-Bagotville Airport in Quebec. The outbreak has drawn attention because the strain is the Andes virus, the only known hantavirus capable of human-to-human transmission. The World Health Organization said Friday it had confirmed six cases out of eight suspected ones and reported no remaining suspected cases aboard the ship. elements_zh.time: 该事件发生于 2026 年 5 月 10 日,该船于 2026 年 10 月 29 日抵达特内里费岛附近,疏散工作持续到 2026 年 10 月 29 日这一周。
elements_zh.location_and_population: MV Hondius 游轮位于加那利群岛,特别是特内里费岛附近。受影响的人群包括近 150 名乘客和机组人员,其中至少有 10 名加拿大人和其他国际旅客。
elements_zh.event: MV Hondius 游轮上的汉坦病毒暴发 导致乘客和船员从加那利群岛撤离。暴发 与三例死亡有关,确定的毒株是安第斯病毒,该病毒具有人传人的 传播 能力。

news.content: 30.10.2026 |Flights of «Türkmen howa ýollary» |Archive | Search Login Main News Shorts Articles Poster Business Media Ads Auto centers Directory Sport Payment Main News Shorts Articles Business Media Sport Payment Place an ad All categories Main /News /World 06.05.2026 15132 Share on social network Spain to accept cruise ship with hantavirus outbreak on board Spain has agreed to accept a cruise ship with a hantavirus outbreak on board. The decision was made at the request of the World Health Organization, in coordination with the European Union, MIR24 reports. The ship is currently moored off the coast of Cape Verde. Its arrival in the Canary Islands is expected in three to four days; a specific port of call has not yet been determined. There are 147 people on board. According to the WHO, seven of them have been confirmed infected: three have died, and one patient is in critical condition. Before the ship arrives in a Spanish port, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) will conduct a situation assessment. Based on this assessment, it will determine who requires emergency evacuation from Cape Verde; the remaining passengers will continue on to the Canary Islands. Upon arrival, all on board will undergo a medical examination, receive the necessary care, and be repatriated. Spain also granted a separate request from the Netherlands: a doctor from the plane, whose condition is considered serious, will be transported to the Canary Islands on a special medical flight. OffOn Stream on News Can I get hantavirus from my pet? Here's what pet owners should know Global race to contain hantavirus outbreak Simpleimages/STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images ByDr. Geraldine Nabeta May 14, 2026, 10:25 PM The recent headlines about illnesses and deaths tied to possible hantavirus exposure have left some pet owners wondering whether the virus can be spread through the furry creature sleeping on their couch or curled up on their lap. While cats and dogs can be infected with the hantavirus, they generally don’t have symptoms and experts say they are highly unlikely to infect their owners. Related Passenger from hantavirus-stricken cruise ship speaks out from quarantine "They can be exposed, but they don't get sick the way that we know people to get sick," Dr. Kate Elden, the chief medical officer of the veterinary telehealth company, Dutch, told ABC News. "There's no actual test that a veterinarian or your local vet is going to have." And even when a dog or cat does have a hantavirus infection, they don’t transfer the virus to humans, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. However, if they bring an infected wild rodent into the home that could theoretically increase your exposure, Elden cautioned. Stock photo of a dog and cat being fed. Simpleimages/STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images "Don't hesitate to call your vet if your pet brought a rodent home and starts to [look] unwell," she said. Elden advised disposing of any rodent your pet has brought home while wearing a mask and gloves, and then thoroughly washing hands with soap and water after it has safely been dispatched. Even owners of pet rats and mice don’t have much to worry about, Elden said. "The domestic hamster, guinea pig, gerbil, these are captive bred animals, we have no documentation that they play a role in hantavirus cases or are part of spreading the disease," Elden said. To be safe, clean cages away from food preparation and spray down bedding to minimize dust particles in the air if necessary, she advised. Popular Reads 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say 17 hours ago 'Inexplicable' order probed as cause of train crash that killed at least 69: Official 6 hours ago Britt McHenry resigns from State Department after basketball game altercation Oct 23 Deer mice are the most likely natural hosts for hantavirus, the CDC notes. Related American who survived hantavirus in 1993 outbreak describes her symptoms and recovery The virus lives in their bodies without making them sick, and they spread it through their urine, droppings and saliva, according to the American Veterinary Medical Association. But your risk depends a lot on where you live. Hantavirus remain rare and scattered in the U.S., according to the CDC, with most cases reported in California, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona. People typically become infected after inhaling contaminated particles, usually while cleaning sheds, cabins, garages or rodent-infested areas or while doing outdoor activities like hunting and camping. One rare exception is the Andes virus, a strain found mainly in South America that can spread from person to person through close contact and has been linked to the recent cruise ship cases. Pets are not known to spread Andes virus to humans. The CDC lists early symptoms of hantavirus similar to those resembling the flu, including fever, muscle aches, fatigue, headache, nausea and shortness of breath. The infection can quickly take a turn, becoming more severe and affecting the lungs. Related Former White House COVID-19 response coordinator answers hantavirus questions The best way to avoid infection is by reducing rodent activity near your home, Elden said. Seal any holes and clean rodent droppings with a disinfectant instead of sweeping or vacuuming. Keep pet food sealed. And if you think you've been exposed through any source, the CDC recommends seeking immediate medical attention. Geraldine Nabeta MD MSc is an incoming chief resident in internal medicine at the University of Connecticut and a member of the ABC News Medical Unit. OffOn Stream on News Can I get hantavirus from my pet? Here's what pet owners should know Global race to contain hantavirus outbreak Simpleimages/STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images ByDr. Geraldine Nabeta May 14, 2026, 10:25 PM The recent headlines about illnesses and deaths tied to possible hantavirus exposure have left some pet owners wondering whether the virus can be spread through the furry creature sleeping on their couch or curled up on their lap. While cats and dogs can be infected with the hantavirus, they generally don’t have symptoms and experts say they are highly unlikely to infect their owners. Related Passenger from hantavirus-stricken cruise ship speaks out from quarantine "They can be exposed, but they don't get sick the way that we know people to get sick," Dr. Kate Elden, the chief medical officer of the veterinary telehealth company, Dutch, told ABC News. "There's no actual test that a veterinarian or your local vet is going to have." And even when a dog or cat does have a hantavirus infection, they don’t transfer the virus to humans, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. However, if they bring an infected wild rodent into the home that could theoretically increase your exposure, Elden cautioned. Stock photo of a dog and cat being fed. Simpleimages/STOCK PHOTO/Getty Images "Don't hesitate to call your vet if your pet brought a rodent home and starts to [look] unwell," she said. Elden advised disposing of any rodent your pet has brought home while wearing a mask and gloves, and then thoroughly washing hands with soap and water after it has safely been dispatched. Even owners of pet rats and mice don’t have much to worry about, Elden said. "The domestic hamster, guinea pig, gerbil, these are captive bred animals, we have no documentation that they play a role in hantavirus cases or are part of spreading the disease," Elden said. To be safe, clean cages away from food preparation and spray down bedding to minimize dust particles in the air if necessary, she advised. Popular Reads 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say 17 hours ago 'Inexplicable' order probed as cause of train crash that killed at least 69: Official 6 hours ago Britt McHenry resigns from State Department after basketball game altercation Oct 23 Deer mice are the most likely natural hosts for hantavirus, the CDC notes. Related American who survived hantavirus in 1993 outbreak describes her symptoms and recovery The virus lives in their bodies without making them sick, and they spread it through their urine, droppings and saliva, according to the American Veterinary Medical Association. But your risk depends a lot on where you live. Hantavirus remain rare and scattered in the U.S., according to the CDC, with most cases reported in California, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona. People typically become infected after inhaling contaminated particles, usually while cleaning sheds, cabins, garages or rodent-infested areas or while doing outdoor activities like hunting and camping. One rare exception is the Andes virus, a strain found mainly in South America that can spread from person to person through close contact and has been linked to the recent cruise ship cases. Pets are not known to spread Andes virus to humans. The CDC lists early symptoms of hantavirus similar to those resembling the flu, including fever, muscle aches, fatigue, headache, nausea and shortness of breath. The infection can quickly take a turn, becoming more severe and affecting the lungs. Related Former White House COVID-19 response coordinator answers hantavirus questions The best way to avoid infection is by reducing rodent activity near your home, Elden said. Seal any holes and clean rodent droppings with a disinfectant instead of sweeping or vacuuming. Keep pet food sealed. And if you think you've been exposed through any source, the CDC recommends seeking immediate medical attention. Geraldine Nabeta MD MSc is an incoming chief resident in internal medicine at the University of Connecticut and a member of the ABC News Medical Unit. OffOn Stream on Officials in Arizona, Georgia monitoring some hantavirus cruise ship passengers who have returned to US None of the residents being monitored in the U.S. have shown signs of illness. ByZoe Magee, Dragana Jovanovic, and Mary Kekatos May 7, 2026, 3:13 AM Share The total number of confirmed hantavirus cases aboard a cruise ship has risen to five as global health authorities work to contain a potentially deadly cluster of the disease. More than 100 passengers remain on the ship, MV Hondius, and the World Health Organization (WHO) is monitoring their health. Officials said that the "overall public health risk remains low" but that there may be some person-to-person spread. In its first public statement on the outbreak on Wednesday evening, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said, "the risk to the American public is extremely low" and urged Americans aboard the ship to follow the guidance of health officials. "Our top priority remains the health and safety of all U.S. passengers," the CDC statement said. "The Department of State is leading a coordinated, whole-of-government response including direct contact with passengers, diplomatic coordination, and engagement with domestic and international health authorities." Officials in Arizona, Georgia monitoring passengers who have returned to US Health officials in multiple states in the U.S. say they are monitoring some passengers who have returned to the U.S. after being aboard the ship for potential hantavirus infections. The Arizona Department of Health Services said it is monitoring one resident that was a passenger on the ship. The Georgia Department of Public Health said it is monitoring two residents who returned home after disembarking from the Hondius. None of the former passengers being monitored in the U.S. have shown any signs of illness, officials said. Cape Verdean police officers stand guard as crew members of an ambulance boat getting in hazmat suites preparing to head to the cruise ship MV Hondius, while stationary off the port of Praia, the capital of Cape Verde, on May 6, 2026. AFP via Getty Images Ship's route The ship, which was off the coast of Africa in Cape Verde, is now en route to the Canary Islands after officials medically evacuated three people, including two in "serious condition." The trip is expected to take three to four days, the ship's operator, Oceanwide Expeditions, said Wednesday. Some passengers disembarked the ship before knowledge of the cluster and are back in their home countries. In some cases, authorities are advising those passengers to self-isolate. The two patients who were evacuated have landed in the Netherlands and "have been received by specialist medical and screening teams," Oceanwide Expeditions said Wednesday. In addition to those two, a third person, who is asymptomatic but a close contact of a German national who died on May 2, was also removed from the ship, WHO officials in Cape Verde told ABC News. The medical aircraft transporting the individual is experiencing a delay, Oceanwide Expeditions said Wednesday. news.content_title: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai Reaches Top 10 as a National Institutes of Health-Funded Academic Medical Center | Newswise
news.content: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai Reaches Top 10 as a National Institutes of Health-Funded Academic Medical Center A different model for medical school and a bold approach to biomedical research Newswise — It was a bold, even audacious, idea—establish a new medical school without the traditional moorings of a university, the entrenched model for nearly every academic medical center in the country. Since its founding in 1968, the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, as it was renamed in 2013, has become a leading research enterprise with an integrated science - plus - medicine formula for success in the pursuit of life-saving discoveries. “This has been a milestone year for Mount Sinai’s research and education enterprises. From our humble beginnings in a vacant bus garage in upper Manhattan to becoming a life-sciences and educational powerhouse, we have propelled science and medicine thanks in part to our passion and grit,” says Eric J. Nestler, MD, PhD, Anne and Joel Ehrenkranz Dean, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. In fiscal year 2026, which ended September 30, the School advanced for the first time into the top 10 medical schools nationally in research grants from the NIH. Ranked No. 5 in North America and No. 6 globally for health care research in the 2026 Nature Index Research Leaders Rankings, Mount Sinai was also recognized this year by the Blue Ridge Institute for Medical Research for 13 of its specialties making the top 10 nationwide for National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding, a reflection of awards garnered in 2025. "We are proud to be one of the nation’s top 10 recipients of NIH funding. The Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai is a free-standing medical school—the only one to stand alongside the country’s leading universities. This accomplishment reflects the exceptional talent and innovation that defines Mount Sinai,” said Brendan G. Carr, MD, MA, MS, Chief Executive Officer, Mount Sinai Health System . "Our unique model brings researchers and clinicians together, allowing discoveries in the lab to move more quickly to the patients and communities who need them most. We are proud to be a leading voice in shaping the future of medicine.” There is no better evidence of the steady growth and momentum it has achieved than this new milestone: placing No. 9 nationally in biomedical research grant funding from the NIH. The Icahn School of Medicine now ranks higher than any other medical school in New York State in NIH-funded biomedical research and has the distinction of being the only freestanding medical school among the top 10 NIH grant recipients. In fiscal year 2026, Mount Sinai investigators secured more than $514 million in total NIH funding across 696 grants and contracts in areas as diverse as the brain, immunology, cancer, heart, genomics, AI and human health, and vaccines and pandemic preparedness. Mount Sinai’s educational efforts are closely aligned with its research and clinical enterprises. The Icahn School of Medicine, Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences, and Phillips School of Nursing are training the next generations of physicians, scientists, nurses, and public health and administrative practitioners. “We were determined nearly 60 years ago to break the mold in biomedical research and education by creating a school within a hospital, one that could build on the hospital’s legacy of state-of-the-art and compassionate care for a unique patient population,” says Dr. Nestler. “Reaching these milestones in a singular year is a testament to our resolve and boldness. Our investigators share a collective ethos—a commitment to scientific discovery, a willingness to tackle difficult questions, and a relentless pursuit of new knowledge—and their north star is making discoveries that become life-saving therapies that change peoples’ lives. That is the ultimate achievement.” In a field where progress has been notoriously slow, few research teams have dug deeper than Mount Sinai’s into the complex cellular architecture of brain disorders that are among the leading causes of disability worldwide, like Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease. Mount Sinai investigators, led by Panos Roussos, MD, PhD, have played leading roles in the global network known as the PsychAD Consortium, which has produced a landmark collection of nine papers enhancing the field’s understanding of why Alzheimer’s disease, for one, progresses differently among individuals. The work offers new insights that may inform future precision medicine strategies. Mount Sinai has also been a pioneer, under Helen Mayberg, MD’s and Brian Kopell, MD’s leadership, in advancing, through decades of NIH-funded studies, deep brain stimulation (DBS). Mount Sinai’s Living Brain Project, an NIH-funded investigation directed by Alex Charney, MD, PhD, was developed to evaluate DBS for Parkinson’s disease, obsessive-compulsive disorder, essential tremor, dystonia, and depression. The surgical treatment, which, involves implanting electrodes into the brain has been a game-changer for many of these common disorders. Mount Sinai is now leading a pivotal multi-site randomized control trial of the use of DBS for depression. Mount Sinai Tisch Cancer Center’s (TCC) designation in 2025 as a “Comprehensive Cancer Center” by the National Cancer Institute represents the highest designation awarded to cancer centers in the United States. This recognition places Mount Sinai among the top 1 percent of cancer centers nationwide and affirms the breadth and depth of its cancer research, clinical excellence, and commitment to health equity. This milestone, along with Mount Sinai’s top 10 funding in cancer research, underscores our sustained investment in cancer science, commitment to training the next generation of investigators, and a promise to improve cancer care. Mount Sinai oncologists, under the direction of Ramon Parsons, MD, PhD, Luis Isola, MD, and Joseph Sparano, MD, have advanced the field on several fronts, including cancer vaccines, bone marrow transplantation, blood cancers, multiple myeloma, bladder cancer, and other solid tumors. Researchers at TCC have led transformative studies across a wide spectrum of cancers, advancing treatments that are changing standards of care worldwide including pioneering trials resulting in the FDA approval of a therapy to prevent recurrence in patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer, an innovative vaccine for urothelial cancer and a new vaccine platform for solid and hematologic malignancies. Advances in heart disease, the No. 1 killer of Americans, have been a critical focus for Mount Sinai investigators who have turned their lens to the less-studied populations of women and children. A newly launched NIH-funded study, led by Annetine Gelijns, PhD and Roxana Mehran, MD at Mount Sinai Fuster Heart Hospital, is focused on uncovering the optimal therapy for spontaneous coronary artery dissection, the disease that took the life of U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham in July 2026. This condition disproportionately affects women, often at a young age, without the traditional warning signs of heart disease. Another research grant for $8.5 million is continuing cutting-edge work aimed at improving long-term outcomes for children with congenital heart disease, while a $10.2 million award is bringing the institution closer to identifying the risk factors for malignant ventricular arrhythmias in mitral valve prolapse. Mount Sinai proudly applauded the appointment in March 2026 of Dr. Mehran, Mount Sinai Professor in Cardiovascular Clinical Research and Outcomes, as the 74 th President of the American College of Cardiology. Autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, and psoriasis are becoming increasingly common in developed nations. Autoimmune diseases affect more than 15 million Americans across more than 105 conditions that can damage nearly every organ system. Mount Sinai researchers, led by Miriam Merad, MD, PhD and Brian Brown, PhD, have focused on new discoveries for patients wrestling with the hallmarks of autoimmune disease, including unpredictable cycles of flare and remission, delayed diagnosis, and limited treatment options, by applying cellular science and precision medicine. This year, the institution garnered a new $5 million private grant to establish the Colton Center for Autoimmunity , with Shruti Naik, PhD, as its director. Residing within Mount Sinai’s Precision Immunology Institute (PrIISM), the center will work with international partners to create large-scale datasets across multiple autoimmune diseases and apply AI-enabled analytics to help fundamentally change how autoimmune diseases are detected, treated, and prevented. The rapid spread of viruses like influenza, dengue, hantavirus, and COVID-19 has thrust Mount Sinai into prominent national and global roles focused on disease prevention. Mount Sinai researchers recently received a five-year award of nearly $21 million to advance next-generation technologies against respiratory threats. The project will begin with an H5N1 flu vaccine prototype and development of a vaccine platform framework for broader, safer, and more durable immune protection. This undertaking will include finding a novel way of approaching influenza in search of protection that is more far-reaching, rather than narrowly focused on a single circulating influenza virus variant. During the recent outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome on a cruise ship resulting in 12 confirmed cases and three deaths, Mount Sinai investigators helped coordinate the international response teams and scientific inquiry that followed. That experience triggered a new $11.8 million federal grant to Mount Sinai to fundamentally change this country’s course of vaccine development. Known as the DOORs project, the research team, led by distinguished virologists Gustavo Palacios, PhD, and Adolfo García-Sastre, PhD in the Department of Microbiology, chaired by Ana Sesma, PhD, is charged with identifying and closing the critical “doors” that whole families of viruses exploit to infect, replicate, and spread. “This approach to pandemic preparedness and vaccine development underlines how we move medicine and science forward, finding new paths and ways of doing things for the good of humankind,” says Dr. Nestler. About the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai The Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai is internationally renowned for its outstanding research, educational, and clinical care programs. It is the sole academic partner for the seven member hospitals* of the Mount Sinai Health System, one of the largest academic health systems in the United States, providing care to New York City’s large and diverse patient population. The Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai offers highly competitive MD, PhD, MD-PhD, and master’s degree programs, with enrollment of more than 1,200 students. It has the largest graduate medical education program in the country, with more than 2,700 clinical residents and fellows training throughout the Health System. The Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences offers 12 degree-granting programs, conducts innovative basic and translational research, and trains more than 470 postdoctoral research fellows. Ranked No. 9 nationwide in National Institutes of Health (NIH) grant funding, the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai is among the 90th percentile of U.S. private medical schools in Sponsored Programs Direct Expenditures per Principal Investigator, according to the Association of American Medical Colleges. More than 6,900 scientists, educators, and clinicians work within and across dozens of academic departments and multidisciplinary institutes with an emphasis on translational research and therapeutics. Through Mount Sinai Innovation Partners (MSIP), the Health System facilitates the real-world application and commercialization of medical breakthroughs made at Mount Sinai. Mount Sinai’s Phillips School of Nursing currently enrolls more than 400 students and offers accelerated BSN programs and a variety of innovative curricula responding to the special needs of working adults interested in entering the nursing profession. ------------------------------------------------------- * Mount Sinai Health System member hospitals: The Mount Sinai Hospital; Mount Sinai Brooklyn; Mount Sinai Morningside; Mount Sinai Queens; Mount Sinai South Nassau; Mount Sinai West; and New York Eye and Ear Infirmary of Mount Sinai

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Cryo-EM reveals how Andes hantavirus grips its human cell receptor by October 28, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 4 mins read 0 Cryo-EM reveals how Andes hantavirus grips its human cell receptor Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Scientists at Albert Einstein College of Medicine, working with collaborators at Institut Pasteur and LSU Health Shreveport, have published a study in Nature showing how the Andes hantavirus recognizes its target on a human cell. The work arrives against a sobering backdrop: earlier this year, an outbreak of Andes hantavirus on a cruise ship killed three passengers and sickened 13, underscoring the absence of approved vaccines or treatments for the virus. The new findings, the researchers say, could inform the development of effective therapies against Andes virus and other hantaviruses. Hantaviruses are a large family of viruses carried mainly by rodents, and they can cause serious and sometimes fatal diseases in people, including hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, a severe respiratory illness that can rapidly lead to breathing failure. Human infections occur mainly when people inhale airborne virus particles from the urine, droppings, or saliva of infected rodents. Of the more than 20 hantaviruses known to sicken humans, Andes virus is the only one known to spread from person to person, typically through close and prolonged contact. This year’s cruise ship outbreak provided a dramatic example of that capability. The research team had previously established that infection depends on the spike protein on the Andes virus surface latching onto a receptor called PCDH1 on the surface of human cells. That receptor essentially serves as a doorway for the virus to enter the cell and then multiply inside it. What remained unanswered was a precise mechanistic question: how does the spike protein actually latch onto PCDH1? Eight years ago the group discovered that Andes virus uses this particular surface protein to infect human cells, but the exact recognition mechanism eluded them. “Eight years ago, we discovered that Andes virus infects human cells by using a particular protein on the cell’s surface, called a receptor, but we couldn’t figure out exactly how the virus recognized it,” said co-corresponding author Kartik Chandran, Ph.D., professor of microbiology and immunology at Einstein. “Our latest work solves this puzzle: We reveal a new way in which a virus can capture its receptor during infection and also suggest how we can fight back with therapies targeted to exploit the resulting viral vulnerability.” The answer lies in an unusual architecture. The spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, is built from three identical protein units arranged in a triangle, each carrying a separate receptor-binding domain that latches onto its receptor, ACE2. The Andes virus spike, by contrast, is an arrangement of four identical protein units locked together into a square. Unlike the SARS-CoV-2 and ACE2 pairing, a single protein unit from the Andes virus cannot bind to its receptor on its own; instead, the entire square-shaped spike is required to capture PCDH1. To see what happens at the very beginning of infection, when the Andes virus first encounters a human cell, the researchers used cryo-electron microscopy to reveal the structure in sharp detail. That step was accomplished only after the team developed innovative new methods, including an artificial intelligence-designed scaffold, that enabled the square-shaped Andes virus spike to hold together in a test tube. “The best way to prove a rare bird exists is to take a picture of it,” said Pablo Guardado-Calvo, Ph.D., deputy director of the Virology Department and head of the Structural Biology of Infectious Diseases unit at Institut Pasteur. “When we mixed this engineered Andes virus spike with PCDH1 and looked at it under the microscope, we knew we had something special.” The structures showed that a single molecule of PCDH1 embeds itself into the heart of the spike by binding into a deep groove, or pocket, at its center. The researchers also resolved molecular specifics of the interaction that will be important for designing treatments intended to block it. “The depth of this pocket also helps explain how the virus limits antibody access,” said Rohit Jangra, Ph.D., assistant professor of microbiology and immunology at LSU Health Shreveport. “What’s striking is how the same pocket can accommodate the receptor while restricting antibody access. PCDH1’s long, slender shape lets it reach deep inside, but most antibodies are too bulky to follow.” The team then examined several antibodies isolated from human hantavirus patients that had previously been shown to block the Andes virus-PCDH1 binding interaction. They found that some of these antibodies could indeed bind close enough to the entrance of the receptor-binding pocket to prevent PCDH1 from entering it, but they could not fit as deeply into the pocket as PCDH1 does. According to Chandran, this suggests a clever way in which Andes virus can escape receptor-blocking antibodies: the virus mutates so that antibodies cannot destroy it, yet those changes do not affect its ability to bind to the receptor, a kind of molecular “friend-or-foe” identification system. That same antibody-escape strategy, however, creates a vulnerability the team intends to exploit. Although human antibodies are limited to a certain architecture, scientists can create “long and skinny” molecules, suggesting an approach that could block the PCDH1 pocket and offer a blueprint for the development of new antiviral medicines that the researchers describe as urgently needed for Andes virus and its close relative in the United States and Canada, Sin Nombre virus. “This work creates a unified picture of the hantavirus-receptor interaction that could help us conceive and discover new protective strategies that work broadly against these high-consequence pathogens,” said Dr. Guardado-Calvo. The paper, titled “Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses,” lists Megan M. Slough, Ph.D., of Albert Einstein College of Medicine as first author, with co-authors including Leandro Battini, Ph.D., of Institut Pasteur and Ramandeep Kaur, Ph.D., of LSU Health Shreveport, along with additional contributors from The Henry M. Jackson Foundation, The University of Texas at Austin, University College London, Ichor Biologics LLC, Norgen Biotek, Universidad San Sebastián, the U.S. Army Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases, and Fundacion Ciencia & Vida. The work was funded by the National Institutes of Health, through grant U19AI181977 (“PROVIDENT”), and by the European Union (EVH, GAP-101202831). As a structural study, it defines the molecular mechanics of receptor recognition and points to candidate therapeutic strategies, which would still need to be developed and tested before any clinical benefit could be established. supplementary_news.excerpt: An expert-rated analysis of 900 responses from ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude found that 88.9% were correct or mostly correct, while 11.1% were potentially misleading.

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Friday, October 30, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Expert analysis of LLM hantavirus outbreak responses finds 11.1% potentially misleading by October 25, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Expert analysis of LLM hantavirus outbreak responses finds 11.1% potentially misleading Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram An expert-rated analysis of 900 responses generated by three publicly accessible large language models found that 63.1% were completely correct and sufficient, while 11.1% were partially correct or potentially misleading about hantavirus risk communication during the 2026 Andes virus outbreak. The comparative, cross-sectional study assessed outputs from ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude rather than patient outcomes, disease transmission or the models’ effects in a clinical setting. Across the evaluated dataset, no response was rated completely incorrect or overtly harmful, but the findings indicate that model-generated outbreak information still requires scrutiny before public use. The researchers submitted 150 predefined hantavirus-related questions to the non-Pro, publicly accessible versions of the three models. The questions covered three areas: information based on official health-authority or guideline material, expert and clinical-practice issues, and frequently asked public questions. Each question was submitted twice, using either a standard zero-shot prompt or a prompt directed toward public-health risk communication. The two prompt formats generated 900 responses altogether, providing a dataset for comparing model outputs and assessing whether specialized risk-communication framing changed the expert-rated distribution of answers. Three independent experts evaluated the responses with a predefined rubric addressing accuracy, completeness, consistency, safety and actionability. Ratings were summarized descriptively, while inter-rater reliability was assessed with percentage agreement and Fleiss’ kappa. Of the 900 responses, 568 were classified as completely correct and sufficient. A further 232, or 25.8%, were rated mostly correct but incomplete, and 100, or 11.1%, were considered partially correct or potentially misleading. Thus, 88.9% received one of the two higher ratings, even though nearly one in nine answers fell into the category that allowed potentially misleading information. ChatGPT had the numerically highest proportion of completely correct responses, with 198 of 300 answers, or 66.0%, and the lowest proportion in the potentially misleading category, with 28 of 300, or 9.3%. Gemini and Claude had completely correct rates of 62.7% and 60.7%, respectively. The investigators interpreted these model-level differences descriptively and did not present them as evidence that one system was superior. The aggregate distribution of categorical ratings also did not change with the public-health risk communication prompt compared with the standard zero-shot prompt, indicating no measured change in the overall rating pattern under the two tested formats. The study supports a qualified role for publicly accessible language models in infectious-disease and outbreak-related communication, but its results do not establish that the systems can serve as stand-alone sources of clinically complex or rapidly changing guidance. The analysis was confined to 150 predefined questions, three public model systems, two prompt formats and an expert scoring framework, and its results were reported descriptively rather than through statistical claims of model superiority. The researchers concluded that these tools may support risk communication when their outputs are grounded in official information and subjected to expert oversight. During a hantavirus outbreak, that distinction remains important because a majority of correct or mostly correct answers does not eliminate the possibility of incomplete or potentially misleading content in individual responses. Subject of Research: Expert comparison of large language model responses to hantavirus risk-communication questions during the 2026 Andes virus outbreak Article Title: Large language models for hantavirus-related infectious disease risk communication during the 2026 Andes virus outbreak: an expert-rated comparative content analysis Article References: Polat, A. O., Tunç Karaman, S., & Basat, O. (2026).
